meta.subtitle: Pivoting arm mechanism · the problem every calculation and every selection comes back to

sections.blurb: What the arm is and what it has to do.
sections.title: The Mechanism

blocks.content:
A pivoting arm is mounted to a structural upright on a competition robot. A motor drives it through a reduction at the pivot. The arm reaches out, picks up a game piece at its tip, and has to hold it there.

**You are sizing it for the worst case, which is the arm held horizontal.** That is where the loads act at their full distance from the pivot, so it is where the pivot has to work hardest. Every number you produce is for that position.

![Fig 1. Pivoting arm, side elevation. Arm weight of 4 lbf acts at the centre of mass, 12 in from the pivot. The 6 lbf game piece acts at the tip, 24 in from the pivot. Not to scale.](attachment:scenario-arm.png)

blocks.title: Today you read this and nothing else
blocks.content: Do not start calculating. In your notebook, write your first read of it: what the mechanism has to do, what you were given, and what you think you will have to work out. You will be wrong about some of it, and that is the point of dating it.

sections.title: What You Produce

rows.d: Forces identified, holding torque, gear ratio, and shaft load. Work shown, units carried, every result tied back to this scenario.
Real components selected from real catalogs and justified against published properties, including a shear sizing calculation for at least one fastener. Plus a complete Bill of Materials.
The whole thing assembled, with your checkpoint corrections folded in.
You present it, and every number and every decision gets challenged.

sections.blurb: The three places this problem is most often gotten wrong.
sections.title: Three Things Worth Knowing Now

blocks.content:
### Torque and shaft load are different numbers
Torque is a twisting moment about the pivot. Shaft load is the straight-down force the bearing physically carries. Both matter, they are not the same quantity, and confusing them is the most common error on this kind of problem.

### The reduction has two requirements, and only one of them binds
Your reduction has to move the arm through its required sweep in the required time, and it has to deliver the holding torque with a factor of safety of 2.0 against the motor's published stall torque. Work out both. Part of the answer is finding out which of the two is actually driving your choice, because it is not always the one you expect. Real gearboxes reach their ratios by stacking stages, and stacked stages multiply. Round to a ratio you can actually buy.

### A large margin is a real answer, and it still has to be shown
When you size the hub bolts you may find the smallest bolt in the shop clears the load several times over. That is a legitimate result and it is not a sign you did it wrong. What is not legitimate is skipping the calculation and asserting it is fine. Show the number, then say the margin is large.
